blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher. Standards and tools change (OWASP Top 10 editions, TLS versions, certificate exams), so check the official source named in the text before relying on a detail. Practise only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

A **penetration test (pentest)** is an authorised, time-boxed attempt to find and demonstrate weaknesses, ending in a report that helps the owner fix them. It is not the same as a **vulnerability assessment**, which lists weaknesses (usually from a scanner) without trying to exploit them.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Black box** | the tester has no prior knowledge (like an outsider) |
| **Grey box** | partial knowledge, such as a normal user account (the most common web test) |
| **White box** | full access to source code and documentation |
| **Red team** | simulates a real adversary against the whole organisation, usually including detection and response |
| **Blue team** | defenders |
| **Purple team** | red and blue working together so each attack improves a detection |
| **Bug bounty** | a public programme paying researchers for valid reports within its rules |

### The phases

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Pre-engagement** | scope (what is in and out), rules of engagement, testing windows, contacts, **written authorisation** ("get out of jail" letter), data handling |
| **2. Reconnaissance** | gather information: passive (public sources, no contact with the target) and active (touching the target) |
| **3. Scanning and enumeration** | find hosts, ports, services, versions, users, endpoints |
| **4. Vulnerability analysis** | work out which findings are real weaknesses |
| **5. Exploitation** | carefully prove the weakness (a controlled proof, not damage) |
| **6. Post-exploitation** | show impact within the rules: what could an attacker reach from here? Clean up afterwards |
| **7. Reporting** | clear findings, evidence, risk ratings and fixes |
| **8. Retest** | verify the fixes |

For web applications, follow the **OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG)**. It is a free checklist of what to test, organised by area (information gathering, configuration, identity, authentication, authorisation, sessions, input validation, error handling, cryptography, business logic, client side).

Stay inside the written scope. Do not test denial of service unless it is explicitly agreed. Do not read, copy or modify real customer data more than the minimum needed to prove a finding. Stop and report at once if you find something dangerous or outside scope. Keep evidence secure and delete it when the engagement ends as agreed.
blocks.title: The golden rules

blocks.text:
You can learn nearly everything legally and for free on your own machine.

| Part | Options |
|---|---|
| **Hypervisor** | VirtualBox or VMware Workstation Player; or Docker for single applications |
| **Attacker VM** | Kali Linux or Parrot OS (pre-loaded tools). You can also use a normal Linux install and add tools |
| **Network** | a **host-only** or **internal** network between the VMs so vulnerable machines are never reachable from your home network or the internet |
| **Snapshots** | take one before every experiment so you can roll back |
| **Resources** | 8 GB RAM is enough for two VMs; 16 GB is comfortable |

### Targets you are allowed to attack (because they are made for it)

| Target | What it teaches |
|---|---|
| **OWASP Juice Shop** | a modern, deliberately insecure JavaScript shop covering the whole OWASP Top 10, with a score board. Run: `docker run -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop` |
| **DVWA** (Damn Vulnerable Web Application) | PHP/MySQL app with adjustable security levels for SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, file upload |
| **OWASP WebGoat** | guided Java lessons, ideal for a Java developer |
| **PortSwigger Web Security Academy** | free, high-quality online labs for every web vulnerability class from the makers of Burp Suite |
| **TryHackMe** | guided "rooms" in the browser, very friendly for beginners (free and paid) |
| **Hack The Box / HTB Academy** | harder machines and structured modules |
| **OverTheWire (Bandit)** | learn the Linux command line through a wargame |
| **picoCTF** | beginner-friendly capture-the-flag competition and archive |
| **VulnHub** | downloadable vulnerable VMs for offline practice |
| **CyberDefenders, LetsDefend, Blue Team Labs** | defender-side investigations with logs and packet captures |

Linux basics (Bandit) → networking and Nmap (TryHackMe pre-security path) → web fundamentals with Juice Shop and PortSwigger labs → one structured path of your choice → defender labs. Writing a short note after each lab (what the flaw was, how it works, how to fix it) is the best revision and later becomes your portfolio.
blocks.title: Order of learning

sections.title: The tools and what they are for

blocks.text:
| Tool | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Nmap** | host and port discovery, service versions | start with `nmap -sV` on your lab hosts |
| **Burp Suite Community** | an intercepting proxy: see, replay and change every request your browser makes | the central tool of web testing. Repeater resends a modified request. Decoder converts encodings |
| **OWASP ZAP** | free open-source alternative with an automated scanner | easy to run in a pipeline (DAST) |
| **ffuf / gobuster** | find hidden paths and files by trying a wordlist | noisy; only on scope |
| **sqlmap** | automates SQL injection testing | lab or authorised tests only; understand the manual technique first |
| **Wireshark / tcpdump** | packet capture and analysis | follow a TCP stream to see clear-text credentials |
| **Netcat / curl** | talk to any port or HTTP endpoint by hand | `curl -i -X POST ...` shows headers; learn it well |
| **hashcat / John the Ripper** | crack password hashes you own, with wordlists | shows why salting and slow hashes matter |
| **Metasploit** | framework of exploits and payloads | learn it in the lab; real tests lean on manual understanding |
| **Nikto** | web server misconfiguration scanner | quick and noisy |
| **CyberChef** | the "Swiss army knife" for decoding and transforming data | Base64, hex, XOR, hashes in a browser |

blocks.code:
# hashcat modes: 0 = MD5, 100 = SHA-1, 1400 = SHA-256, 3200 = bcrypt
echo -n 'welcome1' | md5sum                      # unsalted MD5 of a weak password
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt         # dictionary attack: seconds for common passwords
hashcat -m 3200 -a 0 bcrypt.txt rockyou.txt      # same wordlist against bcrypt: orders of magnitude slower
blocks.title: Hash cracking in a lab (your own test hashes only)

blocks.text: The point of that exercise is the contrast: an unsalted fast hash falls instantly, a salted bcrypt hash does not.

sections.title: Testing a web application, step by step

blocks.text:
Use Burp Suite (or ZAP) as a proxy between your browser and a lab application.

1. **Map the application:** browse every feature while Burp records it. List endpoints, parameters, cookies, roles and file uploads.
2. **Understand the technology:** response headers, frameworks, error pages.
3. **Authentication tests:** weak passwords, error message differences, lockout behaviour, password reset flow, MFA bypass, session cookie flags.
4. **Session tests:** is the ID random? Does it change at login? Does logout invalidate it?
5. **Authorisation tests (the most productive):** log in as two users and a low and a high role. Replay user A's requests with user B's identifiers. Try admin URLs as a normal user.
6. **Input tests:** for each parameter ask what it reaches (a query, a file path, a template, a URL, HTML output). Test for injection, XSS, path traversal and SSRF with harmless probes first.
7. **Business logic:** what happens if you skip a step, repeat a request, change a price, use a negative number, or send two requests at once?
8. **Client side and configuration:** CORS, headers, source maps, secrets in JavaScript, exposed files like `/.git/` and `/actuator`.
9. **Record everything:** request, response, screenshot and the impact.

- **Two accounts, one app.** Most serious bugs are access control bugs, found by swapping identifiers between users. - **Every parameter is a question:** where does this value go? - **Change one thing at a time** and compare responses (status, length, time). - **Harmless probes first:** a single quote, `test`, `../`. A tiny change that behaves differently is a lead. - **Never trust the UI.** If a button is hidden, call the endpoint anyway. - **Stay in scope.** Out of scope means untouched, even if it is reachable.

sections.title: Reporting: the part that gets you hired

blocks.text:
A finding is worth only as much as the clarity of its report. A good report has:

| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| **Executive summary** | one page for non-technical readers: overall risk, key findings, what to do first |
| **Scope and method** | what was tested, when, how, with what limits |
| **Findings** | one entry per issue (below), sorted by severity |
| **Appendix** | tool output, evidence, references |

Each **finding** contains: a clear title, **severity** (CVSS score and rating), affected endpoint, **description**, **reproduction steps** anyone can follow, **evidence** (request, response, screenshot), **impact** in business terms, a specific **remediation** and references (CWE, OWASP).

blocks.code:
Title:        Insecure direct object reference in GET /api/invoices/{id}
Severity:     High (CVSS 6.5, AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N); rated High because invoices contain personal data
Description:  The endpoint returns the invoice for any id if the caller is logged in. It does not check that the invoice belongs to the caller.
Steps:        1. Log in as user A, request /api/invoices/1042 (own invoice, 200).
              2. With A's token request /api/invoices/1043 (belongs to user B). Response 200 with B's data.
Impact:       Any customer can read every other customer's name, address and purchases by counting ids.
Fix:          Check invoice.ownerId == authenticatedUser.id in the service layer; return 404 otherwise. Use unguessable ids as extra depth.
References:   CWE-639, OWASP Top 10 A01 Broken Access Control
blocks.title: A compact example of a good finding

blocks.text: Avoid: "The site is insecure." Avoid: tool dumps with no explanation. Avoid: exaggerating severity. Say what you did **not** test.

- **CTF (capture the flag):** competitions where you solve challenges to find hidden "flags". **Jeopardy** style has categories (web, crypto, forensics, reverse engineering, binary exploitation/"pwn", misc). **Attack-defence** style has teams attacking and defending live services. Start with picoCTF, then join a team via CTFtime.org.
- **Bug bounty:** platforms such as HackerOne, Bugcrowd and Intigriti list programmes with scope, rules and rewards. Read the policy fully. Never test out-of-scope assets or perform denial of service, social engineering or data extraction. Duplicates and "informational" results are normal for beginners, so do not expect income quickly. The reputation and write-ups are worth more than the first payments.
- **Responsible disclosure:** report privately, give the vendor reasonable time to fix, do not publish exploit details early and never extort.

Offence teaches how attacks work. Defence labs teach how they look in logs.

- Install **Wazuh** or **Security Onion** on a VM as your own SIEM and send logs from your lab machines.
- Install **Sysmon** on a Windows VM for rich process, network and file events.
- Run small attack simulations from **Atomic Red Team** against your lab and write a detection for each (a Sigma rule), then confirm the alert fires.
- Investigate **packet captures and log sets** on CyberDefenders or LetsDefend and write an incident summary.
- Practise **phishing triage** with sample emails: read headers, check SPF/DKIM/DMARC, extract indicators.

### Portfolio-sized project ideas

1. **Break and fix your own app:** take a small Spring Boot API, deliberately add five vulnerabilities (SQL injection, IDOR, weak password hashing, stored XSS, missing authorisation), attack them, then fix each and write a before/after note with tests.
2. **Juice Shop write-up:** complete ten challenges and write a report in the format above.
3. **Home SIEM:** Wazuh plus three custom detections and a short README with screenshots.
4. **Threat model:** STRIDE analysis of a system you built, with a data flow diagram and a ranked mitigation list.
5. **Secure pipeline:** GitHub Actions with secret scanning, dependency scanning, SAST and a container scan on a sample project, with a failing and a passing run.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A pentest is authorised, scoped and ends in a report
- Practise only on deliberately vulnerable targets or platforms that give permission
- Burp Suite as a proxy and two user accounts find most access control bugs
- Good findings have steps, evidence, impact and a specific fix
- Defender labs teach detection as much as offence labs teach attacks
- Small written projects become your portfolio

51 original questions on 8 areas. *Recall* questions test a definition or a rule. *Scenario* questions give you a situation, a log or a snippet and ask what is wrong or what to do. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

items.q: *(Recall)* A penetration test differs from a vulnerability assessment because it
o: goes further by safely exploiting weaknesses within an agreed scope to show impact
items.w: A vulnerability assessment lists weaknesses. A pentest demonstrates which ones can actually be abused.

items.q: *(Recall)* In a grey-box web test the tester usually has
o: partial knowledge, such as one or more normal user accounts
the full source code and design
items.w: Grey box is the most common web test, because authorisation bugs need logged-in identities.

items.q: *(Recall)* A purple team exercise is
o: red and blue teams cooperating so attacks directly improve detections
items.w: Each simulated technique is checked against monitoring, and gaps are fixed on the spot.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which document gives a tester legal permission and defines what may be tested?
o: the signed scope and rules-of-engagement agreement
items.w: Written authorisation and scope protect both the tester and the client.

items.q: *(Scenario)* During an authorised test of 10.1.1.0/24 you discover a server at 10.1.5.20 that appears vulnerable. You should
o: leave it alone and tell the client, because it is outside the agreed scope
items.w: Out of scope means untouched. The client can decide to extend the scope in writing.

items.q: *(Recall)* The correct order of the early pentest phases is
o: pre-engagement (scope), reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, vulnerability analysis, exploitation
items.w: You plan and get permission first, learn about the target, then analyse, then prove.

items.q: *(Recall)* Passive reconnaissance means
o: gathering information from public sources without contacting the target systems
items.w: Examples: WHOIS, certificate transparency logs, search engines, public code repositories.

items.q: *(Recall)* The OWASP WSTG is
o: a free testing guide with a checklist of what to test in a web application
items.w: The Web Security Testing Guide organises tests by area such as authentication, authorisation and input validation.

items.q: *(Recall)* After a client fixes the reported issues, a tester performs a
items.w: Retesting confirms the fixes work and did not introduce a new problem.

items.q: *(Recall)* The safest network mode for a lab with deliberately vulnerable VMs is
items.w: Vulnerable machines must not be reachable from other networks.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why take VM snapshots before experiments?
o: to restore a clean state quickly if something breaks
items.w: Snapshots make destructive tests and reinstallation cheap.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which is a legal practice target for web application security?
o: OWASP Juice Shop running on your own machine
items.w: Deliberately vulnerable applications are designed to be attacked in a controlled setting.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which command starts OWASP Juice Shop locally in Docker on port 3000?
items.w: The -p flag maps the container port to your machine, so you can browse to http://localhost:3000.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which platform offers free, structured web security labs from the makers of Burp Suite?
items.w: It covers every common web vulnerability class with interactive labs.

items.q: *(Recall)* OverTheWire's Bandit wargame is best for learning
o: the Linux command line and basic security concepts
items.w: It is a good first step before networking and web labs.

items.q: *(Recall)* Burp Suite acts as
o: an intercepting proxy that lets you inspect, replay and modify HTTP requests
items.w: It sits between the browser and the application. Repeater resends a request with changes.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which tool is used to see and replay a single modified request in Burp?
items.w: Repeater is for manual, iterative testing of one request.

items.q: *(Recall)* OWASP ZAP is
o: a free open-source proxy and scanner that is easy to automate in pipelines
items.w: It is often used for DAST in CI.

items.q: *(Recall)* ffuf and gobuster are used to
o: discover hidden paths and files by trying a wordlist
items.w: They are noisy and must only be run against targets you are allowed to test.

items.q: *(Recall)* CyberChef is useful for
o: decoding and transforming data such as Base64, hex, XOR and hashes in a browser
items.w: It chains operations, which makes it handy in CTFs and in analysis.

items.q: *(Recall)* hashcat mode 3200 refers to
items.w: Modes: 0 = MD5, 100 = SHA-1, 1400 = SHA-256, 3200 = bcrypt.

items.q: *(Scenario)* In a lab you crack an unsalted MD5 hash of a common password in seconds with a wordlist, but the same wordlist makes little progress against bcrypt. What does this show?
o: fast unsalted hashes are weak for passwords, while slow salted hashes make every guess expensive
items.w: That is the reason password storage uses Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 with salts.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Wireshark shows a clear-text POST to /login containing username and password in the body. What does this demonstrate?
o: the application is not using TLS, so anyone on the path can read credentials
items.w: Enforce HTTPS and HSTS. Never send credentials over plain HTTP.

items.q: *(Recall)* sqlmap automates SQL injection testing. It should be used
o: only on authorised targets or labs, after you understand the manual technique
items.w: Automated tools are loud, can damage data and are illegal when used without permission.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which testing activity finds the most serious bugs in typical web applications?
o: comparing requests across two users and roles to find access control flaws
items.w: Scanners are poor at authorisation logic. A human must test who can access what.

items.q: *(Recall)* The first step of testing an unfamiliar web application is to
o: map it by browsing every feature through the proxy, noting endpoints, parameters and roles
items.w: You cannot test what you have not discovered.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A tester changes the request GET /api/orders/77 to /api/orders/78 and receives an order that belongs to another user. The finding is
items.w: The server did not check ownership. Report with the minimum data needed and a clear fix.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A tester sends a single quote in a search parameter and gets a database error message. This suggests
o: possible SQL injection and verbose error disclosure
items.w: Unhandled quotes in SQL and visible errors are strong leads. Confirm with careful, harmless probes.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Changing the parameter `?next=/home` to `?next=https://example.org` redirects the user to another site after login. The issue is
items.w: It helps phishing by borrowing the site's trust. Allow only relative paths or allow-listed hosts.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A tester finds that a hidden "Delete user" button works for a normal user if the API call is made manually. The category is
items.w: The server did not check the role. Hiding the button was not a control.

items.q: *(Scenario)* The tester sees that the password reset link contains the sequence number of the reset request (reset?id=2031). The risk is
o: predictable tokens allow resetting other people's passwords
items.w: Reset tokens must be random, single-use and expiring.

items.q: *(Recall)* A good finding includes
o: title, severity, description, reproduction steps, evidence, impact and remediation
items.w: The reader must be able to understand, reproduce and fix the issue.

items.q: *(Recall)* The executive summary of a pentest report is written for
o: non-technical decision makers, with overall risk and priorities
items.w: Managers decide where to spend effort, so give them clear priorities.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Which statement is the best impact description for an IDOR on invoices?
o: "Any logged-in customer can read all other customers' names, addresses and purchases by counting invoice numbers."
items.w: Good impact statements say who can do what to which data, in business terms.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A tester rates a missing X-Frame-Options header on a static page "Critical". The better practice is to
o: keep the rating to get attention
rate it by realistic impact and likelihood, usually Low, and explain why
items.w: Inflated severity destroys trust. Use CVSS plus context.

items.q: *(Recall)* A CTF "flag" is
o: a string of text hidden in a challenge that proves you solved it
items.w: Typical format: flag{...}. Submit it on the platform to score.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which is NOT a standard CTF category?
items.w: Common categories: web, crypto, forensics, reverse engineering, pwn and miscellaneous.

items.q: *(Recall)* On a bug bounty platform the most important thing to read before testing is
items.w: Testing outside scope or against the rules can lose your account or create legal risk.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Your report was marked "duplicate" because another researcher reported the same bug earlier. This is
o: a reason to publish the bug
normal; learn from it and test less obvious areas, since duplicates are common for beginners
items.w: Duplicates are part of the process. Do not publish the vulnerability.

items.q: *(Recall)* Responsible disclosure means
o: reporting privately and giving the vendor reasonable time to fix before any publication
items.w: It protects users while still ensuring fixes happen.

items.q: *(Recall)* Wazuh and Security Onion are used in home labs as
items.w: Sending lab machine logs to them teaches log collection and detection.

items.q: *(Recall)* Sysmon on Windows provides
o: detailed process, network and file events for detection
items.w: It logs, for example, parent-child process relationships that default Windows logs lack.

items.q: *(Scenario)* You run an Atomic Red Team test in your lab and no alert appears. The right next step is to
o: write or tune a detection for that technique, then run the test again to confirm the alert fires
items.w: Detection gaps found in a lab are exactly what the exercise is for.

items.q: *(Scenario)* You analyse a pcap and find hundreds of DNS queries to long random subdomains of one domain. Which technique is the best fit?
items.w: High volume, long, high-entropy labels under one domain are the usual indicators.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which is the strongest beginner portfolio item for an application security role?
o: a copy of someone else's walkthrough
a screenshot of a certificate only
a list of tools you have heard of
a repository where you break and then fix a small Spring Boot app, with tests and a short write-up
items.w: It shows you can find, explain and fix vulnerabilities in code, which is the actual job.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why write a short note after every lab?
o: explaining what the flaw was, how it works and how to fix it reinforces learning and becomes portfolio material
to publish the solution to cheat
items.w: Do not publish active challenge solutions where the platform forbids it. Write about concepts.

items.q: *(Recall)* A "get out of jail" letter in penetration testing is
o: written authorisation that proves the tester was permitted to perform the agreed tests
items.w: It identifies the tester, the scope and the dates, and is the first thing to show if the tests are questioned.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A tester has two accounts, a customer and an admin. Which test is the most valuable for finding access control flaws?
o: send admin-only requests with the customer's session, and replay the customer's object IDs under the other user
a port scan of the host
test the login page for typos
items.w: Authorisation bugs appear when low-privilege identities can reach high-privilege functions or other users' data.

items.q: *(Recall)* Netcat and curl are valuable for testers because
o: they let you talk to any port or HTTP endpoint by hand and see the raw response
items.w: Understanding raw requests builds the intuition that tools build on.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A finding says "Severity: High" but gives no steps, no evidence and no fix. What is the problem?
o: the reader cannot reproduce, verify or fix it, so it is unlikely to be acted on
it is too short to read
items.w: A report must let a developer reproduce the issue and know what to change.

items.q: *(Recall)* A typical sign that a lab target was meant to be attacked is that it
o: is a documented, deliberately vulnerable project or platform that invites testing
items.w: Examples: Juice Shop, DVWA, WebGoat, TryHackMe rooms and Hack The Box machines.

items.question: What is the difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test?
items.answer: A vulnerability assessment identifies and lists weaknesses, usually with scanners. A penetration test goes further by safely exploiting them within an agreed scope to show real impact.

items.question: Why should the lab network be host-only or internal?
items.answer: Vulnerable machines and attack tools must not be reachable from your home network or the internet, where they could be attacked or could attack others.

items.question: You find an IDOR while testing a bug bounty programme and can see another user's data. What should you do?
items.answer: Stop after the minimum needed to confirm it, do not collect or share the data, and submit a report with clear reproduction steps. Using only your own test accounts is the safest way to prove it.

items.question: Name three sections every good finding contains.
items.answer: Any three of: description, reproduction steps, evidence, impact, severity, remediation and references.

items.question: Why compare hashcat speed on MD5 and bcrypt?
items.answer: It shows that password storage algorithms matter: a fast unsalted hash falls to a dictionary in moments, a slow salted one makes each guess expensive.

items.question: What is a purple team exercise?
items.answer: Red and blue teams work together: the red team runs a technique and the blue team checks whether it was detected and improves the detection if not.
